catalog_locator: Sketch p. 8, §0.2 Phonology (offprint p. 12; volume p. 20); p. 43, §1.3 Commands (offprint p. 47); p. 54; p. 61; §5.4 pp. 135–136. Offprint file (image-only).
catalog_quote: p. 8: "There are three tones: high (written with acute accent), mid (written with macron), and low (unmarked). This variety of Mixtec exhibits extensive tone sandhi, in which the basic tone of words is changed after certain other words. The tones written in this sketch are the basic tones, not the surface tones that result from the application of sandhi rules. This variety of Mixtec is characterized by many fast-speech rules in which underlying forms with two syllables, especially those with the shape CVV, are reduced to a single syllable when they do not receive phrase stress. In this sketch the longer forms are written." p. 43: "Sometimes the stress of the verb shifts from the first syllable to the second in imperative forms." [examples: kíkū sāhmā 'Sew cloth!'; kāxī staa 'Eat!'] p. 61: "Because koyo usually receives phrase stress, the verb that precedes it is often reduced in fast speech: nohō and kīhīn are pronounced nu and kīn."
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog and no existing statements; this is the first statement. It establishes a tone language whose word stress is not described as such, with an implied first-syllable default on verbs and phrase-level stress conditioning reduction. Source located via the SIL OAI harvest (record oai:sil.org:39997 -> sil.org/resources/archives/8798); the Glottolog URL is 404 and the live SIL PDF is could not be reached by automated download, so the file came from the Internet Archive copy of 2023-03-08. Quotes checked against the page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A three-tone language (high/mid/low, with extensive tone sandhi). The sketch has no word-stress rule; its phonology section mentions only phrase stress (two-syllable CVV words reduce to one syllable when they lack phrase stress). The one word-level remark (p. 43) says verb stress 'shifts from the first syllable to the second' in imperatives, which presupposes that bisyllabic verb stems are normally stressed on the first syllable. The grammar also labels clitic pronouns 'poststressed' and 'prestressed' (§5.4), i.e. clitics are placed relative to a stressed host.
new_statements.exceptions: Imperative verb forms: stress sometimes shifts from the first to the second syllable of the verb (p. 43; examples kíkū sāhmā 'Sew cloth!', kāxī staa 'Eat!'). Words without phrase/sentence stress (CVV, CVhV) reduce to one syllable in fast speech (pp. 8, 54, 61).
new_statements.identity_note: Farris 1992 (p. 7) describes the Mixtec of Santiago Yosondúa (district of Tlaxiaco), data from 1969 onward, principal associate Juventino Martínez Cruz, and notes internal variation (u > o toward San Miguel el Grande/Chalcatongo; Nn > ch toward Santo Domingo Ixcatlán/Yolotepec). Farris 2004 is the Yosondúa dictionary of the same SIL team. Macaulay 1996 describes Chalcatongo (de Hidalgo) Mixtec, which Glottolog and hh.bib assign to San Miguel El Grande Mixtec [mig] (sanm1295/sanm1296), a sister language in Chalcatongic, not yoso1239. The 1992 volume also contains Hollenbach's Copala Triqui sketch, which is a different language.

sources.note: States that pitch is significant (lexically contrastive): high and low relative pitches 'seem to be basic', modified by glides and quantity; role of pitch in morphology not yet analyzed; gives four minimal pairs by pitch (ñii skin/salt, ñuhu land/fire, hiin one/nine, yucu mountain/herb). A provisional two-height statement that predates the three-tone analyses (Pike 1948 for San Miguel; Farris 1992 H/M/L for Yosondúa).

[Database: MixteCaSo 2.0.0, github.com/SAuderset/MixteCaSo, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.14980449 (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.10143870), CC BY-SA 4.0]
sources.note: Treats Yosondúa Mixtec as one of 43 Mixtec varieties whose reflexes of the reconstructed Proto-Mixtec tones are coded as ~76 binary tone-change variables (tone levels on a 1-5 scale, contours as level sequences); Yosondúa tone data taken from Farris 1992 (and Josserand 1983). Secondary/comparative: documents Yosondúa's tonal correspondences and changes, not a synchronic description.

sources.note: Tests whether tones change faster / carry less phylogenetic signal than segments across 42 Mixtec languages using coded tone changes from Proto-Mixtec (metric D, hidden Markov rates); finds most tone changes show phylogenetic signal and do not change faster than segments. Yosondúa would figure as one coded variety (tone data from Farris 1992); pp. 11-18 reportedly set out the tone standardization.
